facts.t: **Sudden (acute) dyspnoea** is caused by pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism and an attack of bronchial asthma, whereas **gradual progressive dyspnoea** is caused by COPD, interstitial pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and showers of pulmonary emboli; IPF never causes sudden dyspnoea, and pneumothorax never causes gradual dyspnoea.
**Acute dyspnoea with chest pain** suggests myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism or pneumothorax; an asthma attack causes dyspnoea with wheeze, but chest pain is not typical.

**Dyspnoea with wheeze** occurs in bronchial asthma, COPD and acute asthmatic bronchitis; **dyspnoea without wheeze** occurs in pleural effusion, pneumothorax, interstitial pulmonary fibrosis and primary emphysema.
**Orthopnoea** (dyspnoea on lying flat) occurs in left-sided heart failure, and also in bronchial asthma and interstitial pulmonary fibrosis.

A **localised fixed wheeze** means fixed local narrowing of a bronchus — an endobronchial tumour, an aspirated foreign body, or compression by an enlarged lymph node — whereas asthma gives generalised, variable wheeze.
Wheeze that **disappears with cough** is due to bronchial secretions; wheeze from bronchospasm or bronchial compression does not clear with cough.

**Dry cough** occurs in bronchial asthma, interstitial pulmonary fibrosis and pleurisy; **productive cough** occurs in pneumonia, bronchiectasis and lung abscess — bronchiectasis never gives a dry cough, and IPF never gives a productive cough.
**Rusty sputum** is characteristic of (lobar pneumococcal) pneumonia, and **copious purulent sputum** is characteristic of bronchiectasis.
Hazards and complications of **cough** include pneumothorax, hernia and cerebral haemorrhage; cough does not cause (transudative) pleural effusion.
**Pleuritic (pleural) chest pain** is stitching in character, increases with inspiration and cough, and decreases when the breath is held.
**Continuous agonising dull aching chest pain** is associated with bronchogenic carcinoma invading the chest wall or pleura, not with pleurisy or pulmonary embolism.

**Clubbing** is associated with bronchogenic carcinoma (lung cancer), bronchiectasis, interstitial lung disease/IPF and cystic fibrosis; it is NOT associated with bronchial asthma, emphysema or uncomplicated COPD — clubbing in COPD should raise suspicion of carcinoma.
**Cyanosis** appears when reduced haemoglobin is at least **5 g/dL**.

**Central cyanosis** (including discoloration of the tongue) occurs in right-to-left shunt, marked polycythaemia and interstitial lung fibrosis, and does not improve on warming the hand; **peripheral cyanosis** is caused by shock, cold exposure and peripheral arterial disease, and improves on warming the hand.

**Bilateral congested non-pulsating neck veins** occur with obstruction of venous return — fibrosing mediastinitis, cardiac tamponade and superior vena cava thrombosis — but not as a non-metastatic (paraneoplastic) manifestation of oat-cell carcinoma.

**Superior vena cava obstruction** causes congested non-pulsating neck veins, morning facial oedema, and supraclavicular and suprasternal fullness, with dilated tortuous chest-wall veins that fill **from above downward** (in inferior vena cava obstruction they fill from below upward).

The **carina** (tracheal bifurcation) lies opposite the **sternal angle (angle of Louis/Lewis)**, which also lies opposite the aortic arch; the **transverse (horizontal) fissure** lies at the level of the **4th costal cartilage**.

**Barrel-shaped (hyperinflated, emphysematous) chest** is caused by hyperinflation in emphysema/COPD, with the anteroposterior diameter equal to the transverse diameter, horizontal ribs, dorsal kyphosis (not lordosis), a **wide subcostal angle** (not acute) and transverse shoulders.
**Kyphoscoliosis** causes an asymmetrical chest deformity, unlike symmetrical deformities such as barrel chest.

**Unilateral chest-wall retraction** is caused by volume loss — lung collapse, pulmonary fibrosis and pleural fibrosis (and kyphoscoliosis) — but not by lung consolidation, pleural effusion or pneumothorax, which do not reduce lung volume.
The **diaphragm** is the main muscle of ventilation; **abdominal paradox** (the abdomen moving inward during inspiration) is a sign of diaphragmatic paralysis.

**Indrawing of the intercostal spaces during inspiration** is a sign of increased airway resistance (strong negative intrathoracic pressure), not of intercostal muscle fatigue, diaphragmatic paralysis or pleurisy; prolonged expiration instead uses the abdominal muscles and pursed lips, and intercostal indrawing is a sign of difficult inspiration, not of prolonged expiration.
The **Litten sign** (the shadow of diaphragmatic excursion) is best seen in thin patients, not fatty ones, with the patient examined against light.
Chest **mobility is reduced** (never increased) by pleural effusion, bronchogenic carcinoma and pneumothorax.
**Tracheal tug** is detected in emphysema, where the hyperinflated chest pulls the trachea down on inspiration.

The **apex beat is shifted outside the midclavicular line** by right pleural effusion, right pneumothorax (pushing the mediastinum away) and right ventricular enlargement; right-sided collapse pulls the heart toward the right, so the apex lies near the left parasternal line.

**Tactile vocal fremitus (TVF) is increased** over pneumonic consolidation, a superficial cavity and a cavity surrounded by consolidation, because a patent bronchus conducts vibrations through solid lung; it is **decreased** over pneumothorax, pleural effusion, mesothelioma, emphysema, fibrosis and obstructive collapse (blocked bronchus), and a deep cavity does not increase it.

**Shifting dullness** over the chest occurs with **hydropneumothorax** (air plus fluid giving a level that shifts with posture, with diminished TVF and diminished breath sounds), not with free or encysted pleural effusion or encysted pneumothorax.

**Positive tidal percussion** (dullness moving with respiration) denotes **subdiaphragmatic** dullness, whereas **positive reversed tidal percussion** denotes diaphragmatic paralysis (paradoxical diaphragm movement).
**Unilateral hyperresonance** occurs with pneumothorax, giant bulla and compensatory emphysema; an attack of bronchial asthma causes bilateral, not unilateral, hyperresonance.

The **bare area of the heart** is normally **dull on light percussion** (it is not covered by lung); its dullness is increased by cardiomegaly, pericardial effusion and lingula collapse, and reduced by emphysema and hyperinflation overlapping the heart.

The **right border of the heart** is normally percussed **one finger to the right of the sternum**, and the **upper border of the liver** is detected by **heavy percussion at the right midclavicular line**.
**Traube's area** (normally tympanitic from the gastric bubble) becomes dull with left-sided pleural effusion, a full stomach or splenomegaly, but not with left lower lobe consolidation.
The boundaries of **Traube's area** include the tip of the left 8th costal cartilage (not the 6th), the left 9th rib and the left 11th rib in the mid-axillary line.

**Kronig's isthmus** is bounded by the **7th cervical spinous process** posteriorly (not T1), the sternoclavicular joint and the junction of the medial two-thirds and lateral third of the **clavicle** anteriorly, and the junction of the lateral two-thirds and medial third of the **scapular spine**; its lateral end is the line joining the clavicular and scapular-spine junctions, and the middle of the sternal notch is not a boundary.
A **dull Kronig's isthmus** may be due to a **superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumour**, not to emphysema or a consolidated anterior segment of the upper lobe.

**Vesicular breathing** is a gentle rustling sound with inspiration about **three times** expiration and **no gap** between inspiration and expiration; **bronchial breathing** is hollow, with inspiration **equal to** expiration and a **gap** between them.

**Bronchial breathing** is heard over consolidation, collapse with a patent bronchus, a superficial cavity with a patent bronchus and bronchopleural fistula, but not in bronchial asthma (diminished sounds with wheeze); **diminished breath sounds** occur with pleural effusion, pneumothorax and obstructive collapse, whereas pneumonia/consolidation gives bronchial breathing.

**Amphoric bronchial breathing** is a sign of a **superficial tense (tension) cavity** with a patent bronchus, not of pneumonic consolidation, a big cavity with a relaxed wall or encysted pneumothorax; **post-tussive suction** also occurs over a large cavity.

**Positive whispering pectoriloquy** occurs with **tubular bronchial breathing** (solid consolidation transmitting whispered speech), and is the characteristic feature of a **positive D'Espine sign**, which is due to **enlarged subcarinal (tracheobronchial) lymph nodes** transmitting voice sounds to the spines — not to a paratracheal mass, an enlarged left atrium or pericardial effusion.
**Late inspiratory crepitations** occur in interstitial pulmonary fibrosis; **bilateral basal crepitations with frothy sputum** indicate pulmonary oedema from left-sided heart failure.
A **pleural rub** is a to-and-fro sound whose intensity **increases** when the stethoscope is pressed against the chest wall, and which disappears when pleural effusion develops.
**Consolidation** shows **increased TVF, dullness on percussion and bronchial breathing**; a **superficial cavity** shows increased TVF and bronchial breathing but a **resonant** percussion note.

**Lung collapse** is caused by **total bronchial obstruction** (with absorption of air), pneumothorax or pleural effusion (compression), but not by partial bronchial obstruction, bronchospasm or interstitial pulmonary fibrosis; collapse shows **decreased TVF**.

**Obstructive collapse** shows diminished TVF, dullness and diminished breath sounds with the **trachea and mediastinum shifted toward the same side**; a **mass such as bronchogenic carcinoma** gives the same dull, diminished signs but pushes the trachea **to the opposite side**.

**Pleural effusion** shows **decreased TVF, stony dullness and diminished or absent breath sounds**, with the trachea shifted **away** from the affected side in massive effusion; **Skodaic resonance** and **aegophony** occur above its upper border, and shifting dullness is not a feature of free effusion.

**Simple pneumothorax** shows diminished TVF, hyperresonance and diminished breath sounds with a **central trachea**; **tension pneumothorax** shows the same signs with the trachea and mediastinum **shifted to the opposite side**.

systems.n: Obstructive Airway Disease: Asthma and COPD

facts.t: The main symptoms of **asthma** are **dyspnoea and wheeze** (not chest pain or haemoptysis); the **rapid reliever of bronchoconstriction** is a **β2-receptor agonist**, whereas sodium cromoglycate, nedocromil and antihistamines are not rapid relievers.

**Emphysema** is characterised by **progressive dyspnoea** with hyperinflation: **decreased TVF** over the apices, encroachment on the dullness of the bare area of the heart and on **hepatic dullness**, positive tracheal tug, and an absent apical pulsation.

In **COPD**, the neck veins show **expiratory filling** (raised intrathoracic pressure in expiration), and lung volumes show **increased residual volume, total lung capacity and functional residual capacity with decreased FVC**.

**Bronchiectasis** presents with chronic (years-long) cough and **copious purulent offensive sputum** that increases on leaning forward or postural change, with bilateral basal crepitations that **change with cough**; diagnosis is nowadays confirmed by **high-resolution CT (HRCT)**.

A **lung abscess** presents acutely with fever and cough for a few days followed by a **sudden gush of large amounts of purulent offensive sputum** (increasing when lying on the opposite side) as it ruptures into a bronchus, with bronchial breathing over the affected lobe.
**Suppurative lung syndromes** include lung abscess, bronchiectasis and infected lung cyst; **empyema** is a pleural collection, not a lung suppuration.

**Tuberculosis is transmitted mainly by droplet (airborne) infection**; food-borne (bovine milk) and intrauterine (congenital) spread also occur. In suspected pulmonary TB, the **contact history** must be stressed when taking the history.

Pulmonary TB radiology may show **cavitation, fibrosis and consolidation**; **active pulmonary TB is proved by positive sputum for acid-fast bacilli** — a positive tuberculin test, suggestive radiology or a raised ESR do not prove active disease.

A **positive tuberculin skin test** denotes **infection with or without disease** (not active disease only); it is read at **48–72 hours** and is positive when **induration (not erythema) exceeds 10 mm**.
**Rifampicin, pyrazinamide and isoniazid are hepatotoxic**, whereas **ethambutol is not** (its toxicity is optic neuritis); **rifampicin** causes **orange discoloration of body fluids**.

**Streptomycin** must be **totally avoided in pregnancy** (ototoxic to the fetus, affecting the 8th nerve) and avoided in **renal impairment** (nephrotoxic), whereas pyrazinamide can be used in renal impairment.
**Multidrug-resistant TB** organisms are mainly resistant to **isoniazid (INH) and rifampicin**.

systems.n: Tumours, Interstitial Lung Disease and Occupational Lung Disease

facts.t: **Asbestos exposure** is the main risk factor for **mesothelioma**.

**Bronchogenic (bronchial) carcinoma** may present with collapse, consolidation, effusion, lung abscess formation, or **normal physical findings**; **sputum cytology and chest X-ray** are the non-invasive tools used in screening for early lung cancer, whereas fibreoptic/rigid bronchoscopy and bronchography are invasive procedures.

**Interstitial pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)** presents with gradual progressive dyspnoea, a dry irritative cough, central cyanosis, clubbing and **bilateral diffuse late inspiratory crepitations**; **high-resolution CT (HRCT)** is the investigation of choice for interstitial lung diseases.
**Caplan syndrome** in coal workers' pneumoconiosis is associated with **rheumatoid arthritis**.

systems.n: Pulmonary Vascular Disease, Cor Pulmonale and Respiratory Failure

facts.t: **Pulmonary embolism** typically causes dyspnoea, chest pain and haemoptysis with **tachycardia — not bradycardia**; repeated showers of emboli can cause gradual progressive dyspnoea.
In **pulmonary hypertension** there is a **systolic murmur at the tricuspid area** and **dullness in the pulmonary area**; reversed splitting of the second heart sound is not a feature.

In **cor pulmonale**, palpable pulsations are felt in the **pulmonary area, epigastric area and left parasternal area** (right ventricular enlargement); the neck veins are **congested and pulsating**, with a **giant a wave** and systolic expansion, with tricuspid facies and a positive hepatojugular sign — but **pistol-shot sounds over the femoral artery** are a sign of aortic regurgitation, not cor pulmonale.
**Type II respiratory failure** is characterised by **hypoxaemia and hypercapnia** together (ventilatory failure), not by either alone.
Normal arterial blood gas values are **pH 7.35–7.45**, **PaCO2 35–45 mmHg** and **PaO2 80–100 mmHg**.
**Simple spirometry** can measure tidal volume, inspiratory capacity and expiratory reserve volume, but **cannot measure residual volume**.
In **restrictive lung disease**, vital capacity, residual volume and total lung capacity are all **reduced**, and spirometry shows **decreased FVC and FEV1 with a normal FEV1/FVC ratio**.
